sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Establishment & Nature**: Set up on March 15, 1950, based on the recommendation of the **Advisory Planning Board** chaired by K.C. Neogy. It was neither a constitutional body (no Article in the Constitution) nor a statutory body (no Parliament Act).
• **Composition**: Prime Minister acted as the **ex-officio Chairman**. It included a full-time Deputy Chairman, Finance Minister, and Planning Minister as ex-officio members, along with domain experts.
• **Role and Functions**: Formulation of Five-Year Plans, assessment of capital and human resources, proposing of policy adjustments, and acting as an economic think tank for both Central and State governments.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Directed the allocation of central assistance to states through the **Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula**, which heavily influenced state-level development financing until 2014.

items.definition: Centralized economic programs modeled after the Soviet Union's Gosplan. India completed 12 FYPs before planning was replaced.
The underlying formula approved in 1969 (and modified later) for distributing Central Plan assistance to states based on criteria like population, per capita income, and special problems.
The highest decision-making body for developmental matters in India, tasked with final approval of Five-Year Plans before parliamentary presentation.
Advisory Planning Board (1946), First Five-Year Plan (Harrod-Domar Model), Second Five-Year Plan (Mahalanobis Model), Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) reports recommending structural changes.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Region / Zone Details**: Regional disparities addressed through special category status (e.g., North-Eastern states, hill states) receiving 90:10 grant-to-loan ratios.
• **Driving Advantages**: Special central plan allocations aimed at bridging industrial and infrastructural gaps in backward districts and tribal belts.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: 'One-size-fits-all' approach, micro-management of state budgets, lack of flexibility, and erosion of state autonomy leading to allegations of a 'Super Cabinet'.
• **Policy Interventions**: Complete dissolution on August 13, 2014, and creation of NITI Aayog to promote bottom-up planning and decentralized policy formulation.

items.title: Mnemonic for Classification / Sequence
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'C-N-P' (Commission, NDC, Plan).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Commission drafts plan -> NDC approves plan -> Parliament adopts plan.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly clarifies the hierarchy of planning bodies and avoids confusion between Planning Commission and NDC functions.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember **NEPC** -> **N**eogy Committee (1946) recommended **E**xecutive resolution in **P**rinciple, leading to Planning **C**ommission in 1950.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Planning Commission or the NDC are statutory bodies established by an Act of Parliament. Both are extra-constitutional, non-statutory bodies created via executive resolutions.

Mains Value Addition: Quote administrative thinkers like Paul Appleby who famously critiqued the Planning Commission as a 'coordinating super-cabinet' that infringed upon traditional ministerial and federal responsibilities.

keyTakeaways: The Planning Commission was a non-statutory, extra-constitutional body established in 1950 via executive resolution.
It centralized economic planning through 12 Five-Year Plans and distributed central assistance via the Gadgil Formula and NDC approval.
Its top-down rigidity led to its abolition in 2014 and replacement by NITI Aayog to foster cooperative federalism.
